Pedestrians who are normally sighted, visually impaired, and blind can make street crossing decisions accurately and reliably. While auditory information alone may not be sufficient for accurate decision-making, combining it with visual cues can help improve performance.

When using only auditory information, visually impaired pedestrians significantly overestimated vehicular gap times, suggesting that they may benefit from training to improve their detection ability and interpretation of vehicular gap times. This highlights the importance of considering multiple sources of information when making street crossing decisions.

In contrast, blind pedestrians performed significantly worse than either normally sighted or visually impaired subjects under auditory-only conditions, suggesting that they may also benefit from additional sensory input to improve their decision-making abilities.

It's essential to note that these findings have limitations and should be interpreted with caution. Future studies are needed to confirm these results and explore the effectiveness of training programs for visually impaired pedestrians in making street crossing decisions.

In summary, normally sighted, visually impaired, and blind pedestrians can make street crossing decisions accurately and reliably when combining auditory information with visual cues. However, further research is necessary to fully understand the complexities of street crossing decision-making in individuals with varying levels of visual impairment or blindness.
